hint.p: Remember that the derivative of \sec x is \sec x \tan x.
Let u = \sec\mathopen{}\left(4x\right). Don't forget the chain rule when you find du.
Remember that to integrate something of the form \displaystyle \frac{1}{u^2} you should rewrite as u^{-2} and then use power rule.

solution.p: Let u=\sec\mathopen{}\left(4x\right). Then we take the derivative of both sides to get du = 4\sec\mathopen{}\left(4x\right)\tan\mathopen{}\left(4x\right) \, dx

You can do the next step in different ways, but one way is to solve for dx. Since du = 4\sec\mathopen{}\left(4x\right)\tan\mathopen{}\left(4x\right) \, dx, we divide over to get that dx=\frac{1}{4\sec\mathopen{}\left(4x\right)\tan\mathopen{}\left(4x\right)} \, du Then we substitute back into the original integral. \int \frac{-2 \sec(4 x)\tan(4 x)}{\sec^{2}(4 x)} \, dx = \int \frac{-2 \sec(4 x)\tan(4 x)}{u^{2}} \frac{1}{4\sec\mathopen{}\left(4x\right)\tan\mathopen{}\left(4x\right)} \, du Which simplifies to \int -\frac{0.5}{u^{2}}du

Now, this is one of our basic integrals because we can write it as \displaystyle \int -0.5 u^{-2} \, du and thus we can integrate it. Constants in front just stay multiplied so we get \int -0.5 u^{-2} \, du = \frac{-0.5}{-1} u^{-1}+C Finally, make sure you put it back in terms of the original variable, which in this case is 'x'. So we substitute back in for 'u', which was \sec\mathopen{}\left(4x\right). Thus the final answer to this integral is \int \frac{-2 \sec(4 x)\tan(4 x)}{\sec^{2}(4 x)} \, dx = 0.5\mathopen{}\left(\sec\mathopen{}\left(4x\right)\right)^{-1}+C
